books.section: The Election of 1896 and the “Cross of Gold” Speech
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

primary_sources: Frederick Burr Opper, 'The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,' Puck, August 12, 1896

stimulus.text: Political cartoon, “The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,” by Frederick Burr Opper, Puck, August 12, 1896. A large bearded man wearing a sash labeled “Silver Mine Owner” sits on a box marked “16 to 1.” He holds a small dummy labeled “Bryan” who waves a paper reading “Free Silver Harangues.” At the left, three more small dummies sit in a box, labeled “Tillman,” “Peffer,” and “Altgeld.” At the right, another dummy labeled “Sewall” sits in a box. The caption reads, “If the Show Succeeds, He’ll Get All the Profits.”
stimulus.source_note: Frederick Burr Opper, ‘The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,’ Puck, August 12, 1896. Public domain: cartoon published 1896 (pre-1930); Library of Congress, LCCN2012648552. Labels and caption checked against the image.

stem: What is the cartoon's argument about the free-silver campaign?

options.text: Silver-mine owners, not farmers, controlled the free-silver campaign message
Bryan wrote his own speeches without help from any interest
options.misconception: Bryan is drawn as a dummy moved by the mine owner.

options.text: Free silver would help mine owners and farmers exactly equally
options.misconception: The caption says the mine owner would get all the profits.

options.text: Voters demanded free silver before any mine owner spoke up
options.misconception: The cartoon shows the owner speaking through the politicians, not voters leading.

rationales.A: The owner holds Bryan and speaks through him, so he controls the message.
rationales.B: A dummy does not write its own speeches; the ventriloquist speaks for it.
rationales.C: The caption gives all the profits to the mine owner, not to farmers.
rationales.D: The mine owner sits largest and holds the dummy, so he leads the show.
rationales.general:
Ask who moves and who is moved.
1. The mine owner is large and holds Bryan like a ventriloquist's dummy.
2. Bryan waves 'Free Silver Harangues,' but the owner's hand moves him.
3. The other silver politicians wait as small dummies in boxes.
4. The cartoon argues that a rich interest, not the people, ran the campaign.
Remember: in a cartoon, the one holding the strings is the one in charge.
